title: FlashControl: One-Step Controllable Generator via Distillation-Friendly Single-Stream Teachers

paper.title:
FlashControl: One-Step Controllable Generator via
Distillation-Friendly Single-Stream Teachers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models have become a leading approach in visual generative modeling, particularly effective in text-to-image and controllable generation. Their main drawback is slow inference as it requires many sampling steps. While recent distillation methods enable one-step text-to-image generation, extending these techniques to controllable generation is still challenging. Existing controllable models, such as ControlNet, rely on dual-branch design that make distillation difficult.
In this work, we adopt a simpler strategy. Instead of adding extra conditional branches, we finetune a selected subset of layers in the original text-to-image diffusion model to directly enable controllable generation. This results in DeltaControl , a single-flow, multi-step diffusion model capable of supporting spatial-condition generation while matching the performance of dual-branch approaches. Building on this teacher model, we further apply step-distillation to obtain FlashControl , a one-step model capable of spatial controllable generation with a single forward pass.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 33 , 7 , 16 , 14 , 40 ] have become a strong paradigm for both text-to-image generation and controllable synthesis. In parallel, recent distillation methods [ 8 , 48 , 49 , 26 , 38 , 36 , 29 ] have reduced diffusion sampling to a small number of steps, and one-step generators are now increasingly competitive with their multi-step teachers. Extending this progress to controllable generation, however, is substantially less direct. Existing controllable models such as ControlNet and T2I-Adapter inject spatial guidance through external control pathways on top of a pretrained text-to-image backbone [ 51 , 27 ] . These designs are effective in the standard multi-step setting, but our analysis suggests that they are poorly matched to one-step distillation. When such a teacher is compressed into a single forward-pass student, the student must absorb both the base generative process and the control-specific correction into one computation. In practice, this leads to weak control, unstable optimization, or blurry results, even when the multi-step teacher itself performs well. This observation motivates the first hypothesis of our work: for one-step controllable generation to succeed, control must be integrated into the teacher backbone in a form that remains transferable under distillation, rather than attached through an auxiliary branch . Based on this view, we introduce DeltaControl , a single-stream controllable teacher designed explicitly for one-step transfer. Instead of duplicating large portions of the network, DeltaControl adapts a selected subset of parameters in the original backbone to encode spatial control. We study this design on both UNet and DiT backbones and find that tuning feed-forward layers provides the most favorable behavior for controllability and convergence under a matched parameter budget. Our interpretation is straightforward: in a single-stream architecture, attention layers largely govern global feature mixing, so perturbing them can induce broad and unstable changes, whereas feed-forward layers act on already mixed representations and provide a more stable subspace for injecting control. This yields a controllable teacher that is compact, single-stream, and compatible with standard distillation. More importantly, it distinguishes our goal from prior single-stream controllers such as RepControlNet [ 9 ] and OminiControl [ 44 ] : our objective is not only efficient controllable generation, but a distillation-friendly teacher architecture whose control mechanism survives compression into a one-step student. Building such a teacher is only the first step. The next challenge is to distill it into a one-step generator without obscuring the effect of teacher architecture. Recent methods such as SwiftBrush [ 29 , 8 ] and DMD [ 48 , 49 ] show that score-based distribution matching can transfer a multi-step diffusion model to a one-step generator efficiently [ 49 , 8 ] . In this work, we adopt vanilla DMD [ 49 ] as the main distillation objective because it is a simple and widely used score-based formulation that cleanly isolates the role of the teacher architecture. We leave stronger adversarial variants, such as DMD2 [ 48 ] , to the appendix. This choice is deliberate: our main claim is that teacher design is the critical ingredient for one-step controllable distillation, and we therefore avoid introducing extra adversarial components in the main setting that could confound this comparison. Even with a suitable teacher and a simple distillation objective, one-step controllable students are still fragile. Different controls, such as canny edges, depth maps, segmentation masks, and poses, have very different structures and scales. If we inject them naively, they can disturb the backbone features and make training unstable. We address this with AutoAdapter . AutoAdapter first aligns condition features to the hidden-state statistics, then applies token-wise gating to control how strongly each token is injected. In our framework, AutoAdapter is not just a small add-on. It is the module that makes different control types usable within one model and keeps early training stable, when the student is most sensitive to feature mismatch. A separate issue appears during one-step distillation itself. During late-stage distillation, the student starts ignoring variations in its input Gaussian noise, causing different noise samples under the same prompt-condition pair to produce nearly identical outputs. This hurts both diversity and fine detail. To address this, we introduce a Latent Variance Preservation objective, which encourages the output to retain a meaningful response to perturbations in the input noise. The role of this term is specific to one-step diffusion distillation: it preserves stochastic sensitivity in the student and reduces the tendency toward deterministic collapse. Combined with pure DMD and AutoAdapter, it gives a training recipe that is stable enough for one-step controllable generation. Together, these components form a unified view of the problem. DeltaControl addresses the architectural mismatch between controllable teachers and one-step students. Single stream teacher with pure DMD loss keeps the distillation objective tied to the spatial condition. AutoAdapter aligns heterogeneous controls to the backbone feature space. Latent Variance Preservation keeps the one-step student responsive to noise. Under this formulation, FlashControl is not a loose collection of existing modules. It is a pipeline in which each component resolves a specific failure mode that appears when controllable generation is compressed into a single forward pass. Our contributions are as follows: • We show that naive one-step distillation fails for dual-branch controllable models, while single-flow teachers provide a better foundation for one-step controllable generation. • We introduce DeltaControl , a single-stream controllable teacher that integrates structural control into the base backbone by adapting a selected subset of layers. Across both UNet and DiT backbones, we find that feed-forward tuning provides a favorable balance between controllability, efficiency, and distillation compatibility. • We show that a DMD-based distillation objective, together with AutoAdapter -based condition alignment, provides a stable recipe for one-step controllable generation and preserves spatial faithfulness under structural controls. • We introduce a Latent Variance Preservation objective for one-step controllable distillation, which reduces deterministic collapse by maintaining the student’s sensitivity to input noise, and we demonstrate real-time one-step controllable synthesis across multiple control modalities within a single model. • To the best of our knowledge, FlashControl is among the first one-step controllable distillation frameworks to explicitly build the controllable teacher as a LoRA-compatible single-stream backbone adaptation, rather than distilling from a duplicated control branch.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Diffusion Models [ 14 , 34 ] have surpassed GAN [ 11 ] across a wide range of tasks, including controllable generation [ 51 , 27 ] , image editing [ 1 , 25 ] , and personalized synthesis [ 35 ] . This progress began with LDM [ 34 ] and was further advanced by the DiT architecture [ 30 ] . The recent text-to-image models, SD3 [ 10 ] and FLUX [ 16 , 15 ] , achieve impressive results by adopting Rectified Flow training [ 20 ] , and Multi-Modal Transformer (MMDiT) backbone [ 30 ] . Multi-step Controllable Diffusion Models. Controllable synthesis guides text-to-image diffusion with structural inputs (e.g., edges, depth, segmentation, pose). T2I-Adapter [ 27 ] trains lightweight adapters on a frozen backbone, while ControlNet [ 51 ] adds a parallel control branch and has inspired many variants, including ControlNet-XS [ 50 ] , UniControlNet [ 52 ] , UniControl [ 31 ] , and AnyControl [ 43 ] . To reduce tuning cost, CTRLORA [ 47 ] adapts small parameter subsets of the control branch. Instead of using dual-branch, some recent works, such as UniCombine [ 45 ] and OminiControl [ 44 ] , append the conditional inputs to the noisy latent input and denoise them with a LoRA-finetuned single-branch DiT. These techniques often leverage strong backbones like FLUX and incur a massive computation cost growth with respect to the number of conditions. Despite strong controllability, these methods still rely on multi-step sampling, leading to slow inference. Diffusion Distillation. Diffusion models are slow at inference due to many denoising steps, motivating distillation to shorten sampling while preserving quality [ 36 , 21 ] . Consistency Models and LCM enable few-step sampling but still show a quality gap at one step [ 41 , 22 ] . ADD/LADD use adversarial losses for 1-4 step distillation but can be unstable [ 38 , 37 ] , while DMD/DMD2 distill from the teacher score field for one-/few-step generation [ 49 , 48 ] . SwiftBrush reduces overhead via image-free score distillation with VSD [ 28 , 46 ] , and SBv2 improves further with stronger initialization, efficient LoRA, and a clamped-margin CLIP loss, sometimes surpassing the teacher [ 8 ] .

sections.heading: ControlNet.
sections.text: Text prompts provide global semantic guidance, but many applications require spatial control from a condition map c c , such as edges, depth, segmentation, or pose. ControlNet [ 51 ] addresses this by attaching an auxiliary control branch to a pretrained text-to-image backbone. The control branch processes ( x t , t , c ) (x_{t},t,c) and injects condition-dependent residuals into the frozen base denoiser, usually through zero-initialized layers. This design preserves the pretrained generative capability while learning spatial alignment.

sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text: Our objective is one-step (single forward pass) controllable text-to-image generation via distillation , with stable optimization and high-quality spatial condition model . We hypothesize that one-step controllable generation is substantially harder than one-step text-only generation , because the student must preserve both visual fidelity and spatial faithfulness within a single network evaluation. In particular, the common dual-branch design used by ControlNet-style methods is not well matched to one-step distillation, as discussed later in Section 4.2 . To address this problem, we propose FlashControl , a two-stage teacher → \rightarrow student pipeline for real-time, high-quality and controllable generation. Stage 1: distillation-friendly conditional teacher (DeltaControl in Section 4.3 ). One-step text-to-image distillation methods typically rely on a single-branch teacher architecture. Motivated by this observation, we train a single-branch DeltaControl teacher, which enables spatial signal control by fine-tuning all feedforward layers from the base text-to-image diffusion model. To better handle heterogeneous control modalities, we introduce AutoAdapter , a lightweight conditioning module. Stage 2: one-step student (FlashControl) via distillation in Section 4.4 . We distill the single-stream DeltaControl teacher into a one-step generator using Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [ 49 , 48 ] . In addition, we deliberately drop adversarial distillation , since controllable generation requires realism under a spatial constraint rather than unconstrained image realism. Finally, to prevent late-stage collapse in one-step distillation, we introduce Latent Variance Preservation (LSP) , which maintain the output variation and prevents deterministic mapping.

sections.heading: Is dual-branch ControlNet optimal for one-step distillation?
sections.text: ControlNet [ 51 ] is the most common framework for multi-step controllable image generation. A natural approach for one-step controllable T2I is therefore to (i) train a ControlNet teacher and (ii) apply a one-step distillation method (e.g., DMD [ 48 , 49 ] ). We experiment with distilling dual-branch models, including ControlNet and T2I-Adapter, into onestep generators using DMD. However, the results show that this straightforward pipeline results in low-quality and blurry results, as in Fig. 4 and Table 5 , even when the multi-step teacher itself performs well. We attribute this failure to an architectural mismatch between dual-branch teacher and single-step student . ControlNet decomposes controllable generation into two coupled components: a base denoiser and an auxiliary control branch that injects condition-dependent residuals. In one-step distillation, the student must simultaneously approximate the base denoising dynamics and the control-induced correction within a single forward pass. This entangled objective leads to unstable optimization: the student either collapses to the base model (weak control) or overfits noisy control residuals (degrading fidelity). This behavior is consistent with recent observations in distilling large dual-branch architectures, where additional stabilization tricks are required and training may still collapse (e.g., gradient explosion) [ 6 ] . We further verify in Fig. 4 that simply “simplifying” the objective by freezing either the base denoiser or the control branch does not resolve the issue. Overall, these results suggest that ControlNet’s dual-branch architecture is not well suited as a teacher for one-step controllable distillation.

sections.heading: Why DeltaControl? From RepControlNet to a unified single-branch teacher.
sections.text: This analysis suggests a simple principle: a strong one-step controllable student should be distilled from a single-branch controllable teacher, where control is integrated into the backbone rather than produced by an external branch. RepControlNet [ 9 ] is a representative approach in this direction. It reparameterizes control by replicating parts of the backbone and learning condition-dependent residual transformations that can be merged into a single network, removing the need for a dual control branch during inference. We identify several limitations of RepControlNet. First, it replicates parts of the backbone during training following on a tedious replicate-and-merge strategy, leading to unnecessary increase in memory and computation cost. Second, it does not investigate which layers should be adapted to effectively incorporate control signals. Instead, it adopts a dense “replicate-and-tune” strategy that duplicates and finetunes many layers without analyzing their roles in controllability. Third, RepControlNet is evaluated only on the UNet backbone, leaving open the question of whether the approach generalizes to transformer-based architectures such as DiT. Finally, RepControlNet focuses primarily on a single-condition setting and evaluates only a limited set of control modalities. This restricts its applicability in scenarios where multiple heterogeneous control signals must be handled within a unified framework. In contrast, our method addresses all four limitations. We do not replicate network components but directly finetune some of them, offer more efficient training and memory usage. We perform an analysis to identify which layers are most effective for adapting control signals, design a strategy that generalizes across both UNet and transformer backbones, and develop a unified controllable framework capable of handling diverse control modalities within a single model.

sections.heading: Comparison to other single-branch approaches.
sections.text: Recent methods, such as OminiControl [ 44 ] and UniCombine [ 45 ] , append the conditions to the noisy latent input, offering a cleaner DiT-based single-stream formulation for versatile multi-step control. However, their goal is efficient controllable generation itself, not the construction of a teacher whose control interface can be faithfully compressed into a one-step student. In contrast, DeltaControl is designed around this stricter requirement: it uses selective backbone adaptation to integrate control directly into layers that remain stable under transfer, and combines this with AutoAdapter so that the student inherits a normalized, reliability-aware control interface during distillation. As a result, our single-stream design is not merely lighter; it is more friendly to distill, as will be showed in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Efficient Finetuning Strategy.
sections.text: Inspired by RepControlNet, DeltaControl removes the dual-branch architecture and instead fine-tunes only a selected subset of parameters in the base T2I model. To determine which layers are most suitable for learning control signals, we conduct a series of experiments on two widely used diffusion backbones: UNet and DiT. For DiT, which consists of Transformer blocks combining self-attention, cross-attention, and feed-forward (FFN) layers, we evaluate three finetuning configurations with the same number of trainable parameters as vanilla ControlNet: (i) attention-only, (ii) FFN-only, and (iii) a mixed subset of attention and FFN layers. For UNet, which contains both Transformer and ResNet blocks, we examine three analogous variants: (i) ResNet - selecting a subset of ResNet blocks with the same number of trainable parameters as ControlNet, (ii) Attn - replacing part of the selected ResNet blocks with attention layers, and (iii) FFN - replacing part of the ResNet subset with feed-forward layers. We use Stable Diffusion 2.1 [ 33 ] as the UNet-based model and PixArt- α \alpha [ 7 ] as the DiT-based model. During training, only the selected subset of parameters is fine-tuned. Control signals are injected using a simple condition embedding, implemented as a learnable MLP, and we evaluate controllability using the Canny edge condition. As shown in Fig. 5 , finetuning FFN layers consistently yields the largest improvements in adapting to new conditioning signals across both architectures, compared to finetuning attention layers alone. Notably, this strategy consistently outperforms ControlNet in both UNet and DiT backbones across all training stages. We hypothesize that this effect arises because, in a single-flow architecture, the self- and cross-attention modules already align textual prompts with image features, while the FFN layers mainly transform and refine the combined representations . In contrast, modifying attention layers changes the global mixing patterns of features, where small parameter updates can lead to disproportionately large and potentially destabilizing effects. We illustrate the architectural differences between ControlNet and DeltaControl in Fig. 2 . Instead of training an additional control branch, DeltaControl achieves controllability by fine-tuning a small subset of parameters in the base model, significantly reducing overhead compared to ControlNet and RepControlNet. As shown in Tab. 4 , this design requires fewer trainable parameters, leading to lower GPU memory usage and faster training. At inference time, DeltaControl runs a single-branch that natively incorporates control signals, eliminating the need for a separate control branch. The selected parameters can also be adapted with LoRA, preserving the original model’s generative capability. Overall, this design improves both training and inference efficiency. In addition, we introduce AutoAdapter, which enables effective controllable generation.

sections.heading: 4.3.2 AutoAdapter.
sections.text: A direct addition of raw control embeddings to the model’s hidden states is fragile in the multi-condition setting: edge, depth, segmentation, and pose signals differ substantially in scale, sparsity, and reliability. These differences can cause either vanishing control signals or over-dominant perturbations. To address this, we introduce AutoAdapter , a lightweight module that converts incoming control tokens into hidden-state-compatible residuals prior to backbone injection. Its primary role is twofold: it improves the quality of DeltaControl under heterogeneous conditions and it provides a stable control interface for the alternating student-teacher updates during distillation. sections.heading: AutoAdapter in One-Step Distillation.
sections.text: We retain the AutoAdapter module unchanged during Stage 2, reusing it inside the distilled one-step student. By reusing AutoAdapter, FlashControl inherits the normalized and reliability-weighted residuals optimized in Stage 1. Let the one-step student be denoted as f θ ​ ( z ∣ y , c ) f_{\theta}(z\mid y,c) and the trainable fake score as ϵ ψ \epsilon_{\psi} . In an alternating distillation framework like DMD, the gradient update follows: ∇ θ ℒ DMD = 𝔼 t , y , z , c ​ [ w ⁡ ( t ) ​ ( ϵ ^ ϕ − ϵ ^ ψ ) ​ ∂ f θ ​ ( z ∣ y , c ) ∂ θ ] . \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,y,z,c}\left[w(t)\left(\hat{\epsilon}_{\phi}-\hat{\epsilon}_{\psi}\right)\frac{\partial f_{\theta}(z\mid y,c)}{\partial\theta}\right]. Without AutoAdapter’s alignment, control perturbations fluctuate sharply across timesteps and condition types, escalating the variance of both the student and LoRA fake score updates. By enforcing δ ctrl = g ⊙ c align \delta_{\text{ctrl}}=g\odot c_{\text{align}} , the injected residual is normalized before reaching either path. Consequently, AutoAdapter actively supports faster and more stable convergence in distillation.

sections.heading: Latent Sensitivity Preservation (LSP).
sections.text: While score distillation provides an efficient formulation for one-step generation, we observe a distinct optimization instability specific to controllable distillation: the student rapidly becomes overly mode-seeking. It overfits to a narrow teacher trajectory, loses sensitivity to the input Gaussian noise, and collapses to a near-deterministic mapping for any given prompt-condition pair ( y , c ) (y,c) . Qualitatively, this manifests as late-stage stylized collapse and oversmoothing; quantitatively, it produces sharp, disruptive spikes in both student and LoRA losses during late training. To mitigate this, we introduce the Latent Sensitivity Preservation (LSP) objective. For two i.i.d. noise inputs 𝐳 \mathbf{z} and 𝐳 ′ \mathbf{z}^{\prime} in 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) , we extract the corresponding image latents produced by the student model when using the same text prompt 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and condition 𝐜 \mathbf{c} : 𝐱 0 = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 ∣ 𝐲 , 𝐜 ) , 𝐱 0 ′ = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 ′ ∣ 𝐲 , 𝐜 ) . \mathbf{x}_{0}\;=\;f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{y},\mathbf{c}),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\prime}\;=\;f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{y},\mathbf{c}). (1) Then, we compute the output variation d out = D ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐱 0 ′ ) d_{\text{out}}=D(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\prime}) and the input variation d in = D ⁡ ( 𝐳 , 𝐳 ′ ) d_{\text{in}}=D(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}) , given D D is a distance metric like ℓ 2 \ell_{2} . Our LSP objective is computed as: ℒ LSP = − d out d in + ε \mathcal{L}_{\text{LSP}}\;=\;-\,\frac{d_{\text{out}}}{d_{\text{in}}+\varepsilon} (2) with ε \varepsilon is machine epsilon to avoid division by zero. This recipe aims to maximize Δ \Delta output / Δ \Delta input, discourage the “flat” mapping f θ ​ ( 𝐳 ) f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}) , prevent generators from ignoring the latent noise. In one - step distillation, the only stochastic source is 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , preserving a non - trivial Jacobian ∂ f θ ∂ z \frac{\partial f_{\theta}}{\partial z} is critical for diversity and sharpness [ 24 ] . Crucially, LSP is a bounding regularization rather than an unbounded diversity maximizer. It preserves conditional faithfulness while strictly preventing degenerate one-to-one mapping collapse. The final FlashControl objective is formulated as: ℒ FlashControl = ℒ DMD + λ LSP ​ ℒ LSP , \mathcal{L}_{\text{FlashControl}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}}+\lambda_{\text{LSP}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{LSP}}, where ℒ DMD \mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}} is the baseline distillation objective and λ LSP \lambda_{\text{LSP}} scales the sensitivity regularization. In summary, our complete pipeline achieves state-of-the-art one-step fidelity because AutoAdapter transforms the control signal into an easily optimizable state, while LSP guarantees the student does not undergo deterministic collapse once that control signal dominates the generative trajectory.

sections.text: AutoAdapter ablation. We study AutoAdapter on 3 conditions (Canny, Depth, Seg), comparing: (i) no adapter, (ii) w/o distribution matching, (iii) w/o token-wise gate, and (iv) full AutoAdapter (Tab 4 ). Full AutoAdapter gives the lowest FID and fastest convergence for all conditions. Removing either component degrades FID, and removing the adapter entirely yields the worst and less stable training. We also study how AutoAdapter make distillation converge better in Appendix A . LSP in distillation. We ablate the LSP loss in FlashControl to test diversity/sharpness. Without it, FID worsens (Tab. 1 ), suggesting the loss helps avoid near-deterministic collapse and keeps the one-step model sensitive to input noise. We also compare dual-branch ControlNet vs. our single-branch DeltaControl under the same PixArt- α \alpha setup (single condition): DeltaControl reduces backward time by 50% and training memory by 40% (Tab. 4 ). Finally, FlashControl is fastest at inference, achieving 0.042s per 512 × 512 512\times 512 image on an NVIDIA A100 40GB (bfloat16) (Tab Table 4 ). Additionally, we examine how LSP fight collapse in distillation in Appendix B . Varying Teacher Architecture. Tab. 5 isolates a single factor: the teacher architecture. All rows use the same one-step distillation pipeline with varying teacher model. This comparison shows that the improvement does not come from the distillation recipe alone. Branch-based teachers such as ControlNet and T2I-Adapter transfer poorly, confirming discussions in Section 4.3 . More importantly, even among single-stream teachers, DeltaControl consistently yields the strongest one-step student . This shows that single-stream design by itself is insufficient: the teacher must be structured specifically for distillation. RepControlNet improves inference-time structure through reparameterization, and OminiControl provides a minimal universal controller for DiT backbones, but DeltaControl is the one that exposes the cleanest teacher-to-student distillation interface. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: FlashControl shows that single-step, controllable image generation is possible with a streamlined, single-branch design. It preserves much of the teacher’s controllability while simplifying both training and inference. In evaluations, it performs on par with traditional two-branch methods. For future work, we can investigate simultaneous multi-condition composition (e.g., combining depth and pose in a single input).

sections.heading: Appendix A AutoAdapter benefits distillation.
sections.text: We investigate whether AutoAdapter actively benefits the one-step distillation process, rather than merely strengthening the Stage-1 teacher. We compare the optimization trajectories of the plain single-stream baseline, SS + AutoAdapter , and SS + AA + LSP under identical distillation conditions. Visually, AutoAdapter establishes recognizable structure much earlier in training and yields consistently cleaner conditional outputs Fig. 7 . Quantitatively, it produces lower and substantially smoother loss curves prior to the late-stage instability region Fig. 6 . These findings confirm that AutoAdapter transcends simple Stage-1 quality improvements: by providing a statistically well-conditioned control interface, it makes the alternating Stage-2 updates inherently easier and more stable to optimize.

sections.heading: Appendix B LSP benefits distillation.
sections.text: We examine the training dynamics to isolate the stabilizing effect of LSP. As shown in 6 , distillation without LSP exhibits a pronounced spike in both student and LoRA losses. This quantitative instability manifests visually in 6 , where the ablated model drifts into severe degradation and oversaturationin training. Conversely, the inclusion of LSP yields flat, stable loss curves and preserves coherent visual structure throughout the same training range. These findings substantiate our core theoretical claim: LSP functions strictly as a collapse-prevention mechanism. Rather than acting as a generic diversity heuristic, it actively preserves the student’s sensitivity to input noise, successfully preventing the model from degenerating into a near-deterministic mapping once the spatial control signal dominates.

sections.heading: Appendix C Effect of AutoAdapter on feature alignment.
sections.text: We further analyze AutoAdapter by tracking the statistic mismatch Δ stat \Delta_{\mathrm{stat}} during training. As shown in Fig. 8 , all variants begin from a similar starting point, but the full AutoAdapter reduces the mismatch more quickly and remains consistently lowest throughout training. Removing AutoAdapter gives the highest Δ stat \Delta_{\mathrm{stat}} over nearly the whole trajectory, showing that naive condition injection leaves a persistent mismatch between the control features and the backbone hidden states. Removing either distribution matching or the token-wise gate leads to intermediate behavior: both variants improve over no adapter, but both remain worse than the full model. Overall, this result supports our claim that AutoAdapter improves controllable generation by making the injected control features more compatible with the backbone feature space. All experiments are employed with the same backbone SD2.1, loss DMD only and hyperparameters to ensure fairness.

sections.heading: Appendix D User Study
sections.text: We conducted a user study with 279 participants to evaluate perceptual quality. Each participant compared outputs from four methods (FlashControl, ControlNet, Ctrl-Adapter, CtrLoRA) under the same condition and prompt, selecting the best image based on Image Quality, Condition Alignment, and Textual Alignment. We used 30 prompts (10 each for Canny, Depth, and Segmentation). As shown in Fig. 9 , FlashControl was preferred in 57.3% of cases for Image Quality, 43.0% for Condition Alignment, and 47.0% for Textual Alignment, outperforming all baselines despite using only 1 NFE versus 50 for others. This shows that our one-step method achieves superior perceptual quality while being 50 × 50\times faster. Instant Controllable Diffusion Models. Several recent works share the same goal as ours: one-step controllable diffusion generation. SDXS [ 42 ] distills a controllable student from a multi-step teacher, but still shows a noticeable quality and diversity gap compared to strong multi-step controllable models. JDM [ 23 ] provides a principled joint distribution matching objective over images and conditions, but its training pipeline is more complex, has been mainly examined with a single UNet backbone, and does not directly address the teacher-architecture mismatch that arises when compressing controllable generation into one step. Additionally, neither method has a publicly available training implementation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Dataset.
sections.text: To train a controllable DeltaControl, we use a 2M subset of the Re-LAION5B dataset [ 39 ] as supervised images for consistency with other baseline works. Following ControlNet [ 51 ] , we extract corresponding conditions from the dataset, including Canny Edge [ 2 ] , Depth Map [ 32 ] , Segmentation Mask [ 53 ] , M-LSD lines [ 12 ] , Openpose [ 3 ] and Inpainting. We extract all control modalities from the same LAION images by following the ControlNet preprocessing pipeline on their official GitHub. Some prior works use different condition extraction pipelines (e.g., similar canny settings but different depth estimators), so we follow the ControlNet to unify condition generation across all modalities. For FlashControl distillation, we use only caption and conditions since no image is required.

sections.heading: Appendix J Limitations
sections.text: FlashControl has several limitations. First, although the final student is fast at inference, the method still requires a strong pretrained backbone and a two-stage teacher–student training pipeline, which introduces non-trivial training cost. Second, our experiments focus on 512 × 512 512\times 512 images and six common spatial controls, so we do not claim direct generalization to higher-resolution synthesis, video, or specialized domains. Third, FlashControl currently handles one control type at a time. Our results suggest that training with more condition types under the same budget can slow convergence and slightly degrade quality, so robust multi-condition composition remains future work. Finally, like other controllable image generators, fast one-step inference may lower the cost of creating misleading visual content; responsible release should include usage restrictions, provenance tools, and safety filters.

sections.heading: Appendix L AutoAdapter: Detailed Design
sections.text: In this section, we provide a more detailed explanation of the AutoAdapter module introduced in Section 4.2 of the main paper. Recall that AutoAdapter is a lightweight head that converts a spatial control input ( e.g. , a Canny edge map or a depth map) into token features that can be safely injected into the single-flow backbone of DeltaControl.

sections.heading: Overall data flow.
sections.text: Given a single control image c in c_{\mathrm{in}} and backbone hidden states h ∈ ℝ B × N × D h\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N\times D} at the network head, AutoAdapter proceeds in three high-level stages: 1. Encode the condition image into a latent embedding c 0 c_{0} using the same VAE encoder as the base diffusion model, then project it to the same dimension as h h . 2. Match the distribution of the condition tokens to the hidden-state tokens using the distribution matching module (whitening and re-scaling, as defined in Eqs. (5)–(7) of the main paper). 3. Modulate each condition token with a token-wise uncertainty gate , and add the gated condition features to the backbone hidden states. This design lets the model interpret control inputs in the same feature space as the backbone, while automatically deciding where and how strongly each control token should affect the current latent. We provide pseudo-code for the AutoAdapter module in Algorithm 1 .

sections.heading: Distribution matching in practice.
sections.text: We (i) VAE-encode c in c_{\mathrm{in}} to c 0 c_{0} , (ii) whiten per-channel over tokens as in Eq. (5), (iii) feed the whitened tokens, the current hidden-state tokens, and the timestep embedding ϕ ⁡ ( t ) \phi(t) into a small MLP to predict per-channel scale and shift parameters ( s , b ) (s,b) as in Eq. (6), and (iv) re-scale and shift to produce c align c_{\text{align}} as in Eq. (7). Intuitively, this module performs an AdaIN-style alignment between the condition stream and the backbone stream. Without this step, directly adding raw condition tokens to h h can either drown out the original features (if the condition is too large) or make the control nearly invisible (if it is too small). The distribution matching module keeps the condition in a “safe” range where gradients remain stable across timesteps and conditions.

sections.heading: Token-wise uncertainty gating.
sections.text: Even after distribution matching, not every condition token should affect the hidden state equally. For example, a poorly extracted edge map or an occluded region should be trusted less than a clean, well-aligned region. AutoAdapter therefore applies a token-wise gate g i g_{i} to each condition token c align , i c_{\text{align},i} before adding it to the corresponding hidden token h i h_{i} . The gate g i g_{i} is computed from three signals: 1. A similarity term between the hidden token and the aligned condition token (high similarity ⇒ \Rightarrow gate opens). 2. A time-dependent factor time ​ ( t ) \text{time}(t) that encourages stronger control at early denoising steps and weaker control near the final steps. 3. An uncertainty term produced by a small MLP on c align , i c_{\text{align},i} , which decreases the gate when the condition token appears noisy or unreliable. These three terms are combined into a single scalar gate and squashed by a sigmoid, as described in Sec. 4.2.2. The gated condition token is then added to the hidden state: h i ← h i + g i ⋅ c align , i . h_{i}\leftarrow h_{i}+g_{i}\cdot c_{\text{align},i}. In regions where the condition aligns well with the current latent ( e.g. , edges or poses that agree with the generated structure), g i g_{i} is close to 1 1 and the control strongly influences the hidden state. When the condition is inconsistent or noisy, g i g_{i} shrinks toward 0 0 , effectively turning the control off in those tokens. Their main drawback is slow inference as it requires many sampling steps. While recent distillation methods enable one-step text-to-image generation, extending these techniques to controllable generation is still challenging. Existing controllable models, such as ControlNet, rely on dual-branch design that make distillation difficult. In this work, we adopt a simpler strategy. Instead of adding extra conditional branches, we finetune a selected subset of layers in the original text-to-image diffusion model to directly enable controllable generation. This results in DeltaControl , a single-flow, multi-step diffusion model capable of supporting spatial-condition generation while matching the performance of dual-branch approaches. Building on this teacher model, we further apply step-distillation to obtain FlashControl , a one-step model capable of spatial controllable generation with a single forward pass. Ngan Nguyen 1∗ , Dung Nguyen 1∗ , Quan Dao 2 , Dimitris N. Metaxas 2 , Minh Hoai 1,4 , Cuong Pham 1,3 , Anh Tran 1 1 Qualcomm AI Research 2 Rutgers University 3 Posts and Telecommunications Institute of Technology 4 Adelaide University {ngannguy,dungtien,minhhoai,pcuong,anhtra}@qti.qualcomm.com quan.dao@rutgers.edu, dnm@cs.rutgers.edu Figure 1 : Our controllable image generator, FlashControl , turns spatial conditions into high-quality images in just a single step. 1 Introduction Diffusion models [ 33 , 7 , 16 , 14 , 40 ] have become a strong paradigm for both text-to-image generation and controllable synthesis. In parallel, recent distillation methods [ 8 , 48 , 49 , 26 , 38 , 36 , 29 ] have reduced diffusion sampling to a small number of steps, and one-step generators are now increasingly competitive with their multi-step teachers. Extending this progress to controllable generation, however, is substantially less direct. Existing controllable models such as ControlNet and T2I-Adapter inject spatial guidance through external control pathways on top of a pretrained text-to-image backbone [ 51 , 27 ] . These designs are effective in the standard multi-step setting, but our analysis suggests that they are poorly matched to one-step distillation. When such a teacher is compressed into a single forward-pass student, the student must absorb both the base generative process and the control-specific correction into one computation. In practice, this leads to weak control, unstable optimization, or blurry results, even when the multi-step teacher itself performs well. This observation motivates the first hypothesis of our work: for one-step controllable generation to succeed, control must be integrated into the teacher backbone in a form that remains transferable under distillation, rather than attached through an auxiliary branch . Based on this view, we introduce DeltaControl , a single-stream controllable teacher designed explicitly for one-step transfer. Instead of duplicating large portions of the network, DeltaControl adapts a selected subset of parameters in the original backbone to encode spatial control. We study this design on both UNet and DiT backbones and find that tuning feed-forward layers provides the most favorable behavior for controllability and convergence under a matched parameter budget. Our interpretation is straightforward: in a single-stream architecture, attention layers largely govern global feature mixing, so perturbing them can induce broad and unstable changes, whereas feed-forward layers act on already mixed representations and provide a more stable subspace for injecting control. This yields a controllable teacher that is compact, single-stream, and compatible with standard distillation. More importantly, it distinguishes our goal from prior single-stream controllers such as RepControlNet [ 9 ] and OminiControl [ 44 ] : our objective is not only efficient controllable generation, but a distillation-friendly teacher architecture whose control mechanism survives compression into a one-step student. Building such a teacher is only the first step. The next challenge is to distill it into a one-step generator without obscuring the effect of teacher architecture. Recent methods such as SwiftBrush [ 29 , 8 ] and DMD [ 48 , 49 ] show that score-based distribution matching can transfer a multi-step diffusion model to a one-step generator efficiently [ 49 , 8 ] . In this work, we adopt vanilla DMD [ 49 ] as the main distillation objective because it is a simple and widely used score-based formulation that cleanly isolates the role of the teacher architecture. We leave stronger adversarial variants, such as DMD2 [ 48 ] , to the appendix. This choice is deliberate: our main claim is that teacher design is the critical ingredient for one-step controllable distillation, and we therefore avoid introducing extra adversarial components in the main setting that could confound this comparison. Even with a suitable teacher and a simple distillation objective, one-step controllable students are still fragile. Different controls, such as canny edges, depth maps, segmentation masks, and poses, have very different structures and scales. If we inject them naively, they can disturb the backbone features and make training unstable. We address this with AutoAdapter . AutoAdapter first aligns condition features to the hidden-state statistics, then applies token-wise gating to control how strongly each token is injected. In our framework, AutoAdapter is not just a small add-on. It is the module that makes different control types usable within one model and keeps early training stable, when the student is most sensitive to feature mismatch. A separate issue appears during one-step distillation itself. During late-stage distillation, the student starts ignoring variations in its input Gaussian noise, causing different noise samples under the same prompt-condition pair to produce nearly identical outputs. This hurts both diversity and fine detail. To address this, we introduce a Latent Variance Preservation objective, which encourages the output to retain a meaningful response to perturbations in the input noise. The role of this term is specific to one-step diffusion distillation: it preserves stochastic sensitivity in the student and reduces the tendency toward deterministic collapse. Combined with pure DMD and AutoAdapter, it gives a training recipe that is stable enough for one-step controllable generation. Together, these components form a unified view of the problem. DeltaControl addresses the architectural mismatch between controllable teachers and one-step students. Single stream teacher with pure DMD loss keeps the distillation objective tied to the spatial condition. AutoAdapter aligns heterogeneous controls to the backbone feature space. Latent Variance Preservation keeps the one-step student responsive to noise. Under this formulation, FlashControl is not a loose collection of existing modules. It is a pipeline in which each component resolves a specific failure mode that appears when controllable generation is compressed into a single forward pass. Our contributions are as follows: • We show that naive one-step distillation fails for dual-branch controllable models, while single-flow teachers provide a better foundation for one-step controllable generation. • We introduce DeltaControl , a single-stream controllable teacher that integrates structural control into the base backbone by adapting a selected subset of layers. Across both UNet and DiT backbones, we find that feed-forward tuning provides a favorable balance between controllability, efficiency, and distillation compatibility. • We show that a DMD-based distillation objective, together with AutoAdapter -based condition alignment, provides a stable recipe for one-step controllable generation and preserves spatial faithfulness under structural controls. • We introduce a Latent Variance Preservation objective for one-step controllable distillation, which reduces deterministic collapse by maintaining the student’s sensitivity to input noise, and we demonstrate real-time one-step controllable synthesis across multiple control modalities within a single model. • To the best of our knowledge, FlashControl is among the first one-step controllable distillation frameworks to explicitly build the controllable teacher as a LoRA-compatible single-stream backbone adaptation, rather than distilling from a duplicated control branch. 2 Related Work Diffusion Models [ 14 , 34 ] have surpassed GAN [ 11 ] across a wide range of tasks, including controllable generation [ 51 , 27 ] , image editing [ 1 , 25 ] , and personalized synthesis [ 35 ] . This progress began with LDM [ 34 ] and was further advanced by the DiT architecture [ 30 ] . The recent text-to-image models, SD3 [ 10 ] and FLUX [ 16 , 15 ] , achieve impressive results by adopting Rectified Flow training [ 20 ] , and Multi-Modal Transformer (MMDiT) backbone [ 30 ] . Multi-step Controllable Diffusion Models. Controllable synthesis guides text-to-image diffusion with structural inputs (e.g., edges, depth, segmentation, pose). T2I-Adapter [ 27 ] trains lightweight adapters on a frozen backbone, while ControlNet [ 51 ] adds a parallel control branch and has inspired many variants, including ControlNet-XS [ 50 ] , UniControlNet [ 52 ] , UniControl [ 31 ] , and AnyControl [ 43 ] . To reduce tuning cost, CTRLORA [ 47 ] adapts small parameter subsets of the control branch. Instead of using dual-branch, some recent works, such as UniCombine [ 45 ] and OminiControl [ 44 ] , append the conditional inputs to the noisy latent input and denoise them with a LoRA-finetuned single-branch DiT. These techniques often leverage strong backbones like FLUX and incur a massive computation cost growth with respect to the number of conditions. Despite strong controllability, these methods still rely on multi-step sampling, leading to slow inference. Diffusion Distillation. Diffusion models are slow at inference due to many denoising steps, motivating distillation to shorten sampling while preserving quality [ 36 , 21 ] . Consistency Models and LCM enable few-step sampling but still show a quality gap at one step [ 41 , 22 ] . ADD/LADD use adversarial losses for 1-4 step distillation but can be unstable [ 38 , 37 ] , while DMD/DMD2 distill from the teacher score field for one-/few-step generation [ 49 , 48 ] . SwiftBrush reduces overhead via image-free score distillation with VSD [ 28 , 46 ] , and SBv2 improves further with stronger initialization, efficient LoRA, and a clamped-margin CLIP loss, sometimes surpassing the teacher [ 8 ] . 3 Preliminaries Figure 2 : Comparison of ControlNet (a) and our proposal DeltaControl (b). The architecture of AutoAdapter is illustrated in (c). Diffusion and Flow-based Generative Models. Modern text-to-image models generate images by learning to map a noisy sample back to clean data. At inference, sampling starts from Gaussian noise and repeatedly applies the learned denoising or flow field, which yields high quality but requires many network evaluations. ControlNet. Text prompts provide global semantic guidance, but many applications require spatial control from a condition map c c , such as edges, depth, segmentation, or pose. ControlNet [ 51 ] addresses this by attaching an auxiliary control branch to a pretrained text-to-image backbone. The control branch processes ( x t , t , c ) (x_{t},t,c) and injects condition-dependent residuals into the frozen base denoiser, usually through zero-initialized layers. This design preserves the pretrained generative capability while learning spatial alignment. Distribution Matching Distillation. We use Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [ 49 , 48 ] as our main one-step distillation objective. DMD trains a generator G θ G_{\theta} to match the distribution of a pretrained diffusion teacher without simulating the full teacher trajectory at inference. Given input noise z z , text prompt y y , and spatial condition c c , the student predicts x ^ 0 = G θ ​ ( z , y , c ) . \hat{x}_{0}=G_{\theta}(z,y,c). The student output is then noised to timestep t t to obtain x t x_{t} . DMD updates the student using the score discrepancy between a frozen teacher score estimator ϵ ϕ \epsilon_{\phi} and a trainable fake score estimator ϵ ψ \epsilon_{\psi} : ∇ θ ℒ DMD = 𝔼 z , ϵ , t , y , c ​ [ w ⁡ ( t ) ​ ( ϵ ϕ ​ ( x t , t , y , c ) − ϵ ψ ​ ( x t , t , y , c ) ) ​ ∂ G θ ​ ( z , y , c ) ∂ θ ] , \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}=\mathbb{E}_{z,\epsilon,t,y,c}\left[w(t)\left(\epsilon_{\phi}(x_{t},t,y,c)-\epsilon_{\psi}(x_{t},t,y,c)\right)\frac{\partial G_{\theta}(z,y,c)}{\partial\theta}\right], where w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) is a timestep-dependent weighting function. 4 FlashControl 4.1 Overview Our objective is one-step (single forward pass) controllable text-to-image generation via distillation , with stable optimization and high-quality spatial condition model . We hypothesize that one-step controllable generation is substantially harder than one-step text-only generation , because the student must preserve both visual fidelity and spatial faithfulness within a single network evaluation. In particular, the common dual-branch design used by ControlNet-style methods is not well matched to one-step distillation, as discussed later in Section 4.2 . To address this problem, we propose FlashControl , a two-stage teacher → \rightarrow student pipeline for real-time, high-quality and controllable generation. Stage 1: distillation-friendly conditional teacher (DeltaControl in Section 4.3 ). One-step text-to-image distillation methods typically rely on a single-branch teacher architecture. Motivated by this observation, we train a single-branch DeltaControl teacher, which enables spatial signal control by fine-tuning all feedforward layers from the base text-to-image diffusion model. To better handle heterogeneous control modalities, we introduce AutoAdapter , a lightweight conditioning module. Stage 2: one-step student (FlashControl) via distillation in Section 4.4 . We distill the single-stream DeltaControl teacher into a one-step generator using Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [ 49 , 48 ] . In addition, we deliberately drop adversarial distillation , since controllable generation requires realism under a spatial constraint rather than unconstrained image realism. Finally, to prevent late-stage collapse in one-step distillation, we introduce Latent Variance Preservation (LSP) , which maintain the output variation and prevents deterministic mapping. 4.2 From Dual-branch to efficient single-stream teacher. Is dual-branch ControlNet optimal for one-step distillation? ControlNet [ 51 ] is the most common framework for multi-step controllable image generation. A natural approach for one-step controllable T2I is therefore to (i) train a ControlNet teacher and (ii) apply a one-step distillation method (e.g., DMD [ 48 , 49 ] ). We experiment with distilling dual-branch models, including ControlNet and T2I-Adapter, into onestep generators using DMD. However, the results show that this straightforward pipeline results in low-quality and blurry results, as in Fig. 4 and Table 5 , even when the multi-step teacher itself performs well. We attribute this failure to an architectural mismatch between dual-branch teacher and single-step student . ControlNet decomposes controllable generation into two coupled components: a base denoiser and an auxiliary control branch that injects condition-dependent residuals. In one-step distillation, the student must simultaneously approximate the base denoising dynamics and the control-induced correction within a single forward pass. This entangled objective leads to unstable optimization: the student either collapses to the base model (weak control) or overfits noisy control residuals (degrading fidelity). This behavior is consistent with recent observations in distilling large dual-branch architectures, where additional stabilization tricks are required and training may still collapse (e.g., gradient explosion) [ 6 ] . We further verify in Fig. 4 that simply “simplifying” the objective by freezing either the base denoiser or the control branch does not resolve the issue. Overall, these results suggest that ControlNet’s dual-branch architecture is not well suited as a teacher for one-step controllable distillation. Why DeltaControl? From RepControlNet to a unified single-branch teacher. This analysis suggests a simple principle: a strong one-step controllable student should be distilled from a single-branch controllable teacher, where control is integrated into the backbone rather than produced by an external branch. RepControlNet [ 9 ] is a representative approach in this direction. It reparameterizes control by replicating parts of the backbone and learning condition-dependent residual transformations that can be merged into a single network, removing the need for a dual control branch during inference. We identify several limitations of RepControlNet. First, it replicates parts of the backbone during training following on a tedious replicate-and-merge strategy, leading to unnecessary increase in memory and computation cost. Second, it does not investigate which layers should be adapted to effectively incorporate control signals. Instead, it adopts a dense “replicate-and-tune” strategy that duplicates and finetunes many layers without analyzing their roles in controllability. Third, RepControlNet is evaluated only on the UNet backbone, leaving open the question of whether the approach generalizes to transformer-based architectures such as DiT. Finally, RepControlNet focuses primarily on a single-condition setting and evaluates only a limited set of control modalities. This restricts its applicability in scenarios where multiple heterogeneous control signals must be handled within a unified framework. In contrast, our method addresses all four limitations. We do not replicate network components but directly finetune some of them, offer more efficient training and memory usage. We perform an analysis to identify which layers are most effective for adapting control signals, design a strategy that generalizes across both UNet and transformer backbones, and develop a unified controllable framework capable of handling diverse control modalities within a single model. Comparison to other single-branch approaches. Recent methods, such as OminiControl [ 44 ] and UniCombine [ 45 ] , append the conditions to the noisy latent input, offering a cleaner DiT-based single-stream formulation for versatile multi-step control. However, their goal is efficient controllable generation itself, not the construction of a teacher whose control interface can be faithfully compressed into a one-step student. In contrast, DeltaControl is designed around this stricter requirement: it uses selective backbone adaptation to integrate control directly into layers that remain stable under transfer, and combines this with AutoAdapter so that the student inherits a normalized, reliability-aware control interface during distillation. As a result, our single-stream design is not merely lighter; it is more friendly to distill, as will be showed in Section 5 . 4.3 Stage 1: DeltaControl - Multi-step Conditional Model 4.3.1 Efficient Finetuning Strategy. Inspired by RepControlNet, DeltaControl removes the dual-branch architecture and instead fine-tunes only a selected subset of parameters in the base T2I model. To determine which layers are most suitable for learning control signals, we conduct a series of experiments on two widely used diffusion backbones: UNet and DiT. For DiT, which consists of Transformer blocks combining self-attention, cross-attention, and feed-forward (FFN) layers, we evaluate three finetuning configurations with the same number of trainable parameters as vanilla ControlNet: (i) attention-only, (ii) FFN-only, and (iii) a mixed subset of attention and FFN layers. For UNet, which contains both Transformer and ResNet blocks, we examine three analogous variants: (i) ResNet - selecting a subset of ResNet blocks with the same number of trainable parameters as ControlNet, (ii) Attn - replacing part of the selected ResNet blocks with attention layers, and (iii) FFN - replacing part of the ResNet subset with feed-forward layers. We use Stable Diffusion 2.1 [ 33 ] as the UNet-based model and PixArt- α \alpha [ 7 ] as the DiT-based model. During training, only the selected subset of parameters is fine-tuned. Control signals are injected using a simple condition embedding, implemented as a learnable MLP, and we evaluate controllability using the Canny edge condition. As shown in Fig. 5 , finetuning FFN layers consistently yields the largest improvements in adapting to new conditioning signals across both architectures, compared to finetuning attention layers alone. Notably, this strategy consistently outperforms ControlNet in both UNet and DiT backbones across all training stages. We hypothesize that this effect arises because, in a single-flow architecture, the self- and cross-attention modules already align textual prompts with image features, while the FFN layers mainly transform and refine the combined representations . In contrast, modifying attention layers changes the global mixing patterns of features, where small parameter updates can lead to disproportionately large and potentially destabilizing effects. We illustrate the architectural differences between ControlNet and DeltaControl in Fig. 2 . Instead of training an additional control branch, DeltaControl achieves controllability by fine-tuning a small subset of parameters in the base model, significantly reducing overhead compared to ControlNet and RepControlNet. As shown in Tab. 4 , this design requires fewer trainable parameters, leading to lower GPU memory usage and faster training. At inference time, DeltaControl runs a single-branch that natively incorporates control signals, eliminating the need for a separate control branch. The selected parameters can also be adapted with LoRA, preserving the original model’s generative capability. Overall, this design improves both training and inference efficiency. In addition, we introduce AutoAdapter, which enables effective controllable generation. 4.3.2 AutoAdapter. A direct addition of raw control embeddings to the model’s hidden states is fragile in the multi-condition setting: edge, depth, segmentation, and pose signals differ substantially in scale, sparsity, and reliability. These differences can cause either vanishing control signals or over-dominant perturbations. To address this, we introduce AutoAdapter , a lightweight module that converts incoming control tokens into hidden-state-compatible residuals prior to backbone injection. Its primary role is twofold: it improves the quality of DeltaControl under heterogeneous conditions and it provides a stable control interface for the alternating student-teacher updates during distillation. While score distillation provides an efficient formulation for one-step generation, we observe a distinct optimization instability specific to controllable distillation: the student rapidly becomes overly mode-seeking. It overfits to a narrow teacher trajectory, loses sensitivity to the input Gaussian noise, and collapses to a near-deterministic mapping for any given prompt-condition pair ( y , c ) (y,c) . Qualitatively, this manifests as late-stage stylized collapse and oversmoothing; quantitatively, it produces sharp, disruptive spikes in both student and LoRA losses during late training. To mitigate this, we introduce the Latent Sensitivity Preservation (LSP) objective. For two i.i.d. noise inputs 𝐳 \mathbf{z} and 𝐳 ′ \mathbf{z}^{\prime} in 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) , we extract the corresponding image latents produced by the student model when using the same text prompt 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and condition 𝐜 \mathbf{c} : 𝐱 0 = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 ∣ 𝐲 , 𝐜 ) , 𝐱 0 ′ = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 ′ ∣ 𝐲 , 𝐜 ) . \mathbf{x}_{0}\;=\;f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{y},\mathbf{c}),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\prime}\;=\;f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{y},\mathbf{c}). (1) Then, we compute the output variation d out = D ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐱 0 ′ ) d_{\text{out}}=D(\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\prime}) and the input variation d in = D ⁡ ( 𝐳 , 𝐳 ′ ) d_{\text{in}}=D(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}) , given D D is a distance metric like ℓ 2 \ell_{2} . Our LSP objective is computed as: ℒ LSP = − d out d in + ε \mathcal{L}_{\text{LSP}}\;=\;-\,\frac{d_{\text{out}}}{d_{\text{in}}+\varepsilon} (2) with ε \varepsilon is machine epsilon to avoid division by zero. This recipe aims to maximize Δ \Delta output / Δ \Delta input, discourage the “flat” mapping f θ ​ ( 𝐳 ) f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}) , prevent generators from ignoring the latent noise. In one - step distillation, the only stochastic source is 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , preserving a non - trivial Jacobian ∂ f θ ∂ z \frac{\partial f_{\theta}}{\partial z} is critical for diversity and sharpness [ 24 ] . Crucially, LSP is a bounding regularization rather than an unbounded diversity maximizer. It preserves conditional faithfulness while strictly preventing degenerate one-to-one mapping collapse. The final FlashControl objective is formulated as: ℒ FlashControl = ℒ DMD + λ LSP ​ ℒ LSP , \mathcal{L}_{\text{FlashControl}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}}+\lambda_{\text{LSP}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{LSP}}, where ℒ DMD \mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}} is the baseline distillation objective and λ LSP \lambda_{\text{LSP}} scales the sensitivity regularization.
